stem: In LangChain's multi-agent guide, one pattern has a main agent that calls specialised agents as tools, so every routing decision passes through that main agent. Which pattern is it?

options.text: Handoffs
options.why: Handoffs change behaviour through a state variable such as `active_agent`, and the active agent talks to the user directly; no single agent sits in the middle of every turn.

options.text: Subagents
options.why: The main agent, often called the supervisor, decides which subagent tool to call, what input to give it and how to combine the results.

options.text: Skills
options.why: Skills keep one agent in control and load specialised prompts on demand; there are no separate agents to route between.

options.text: Router
options.why: A router is a classification step that dispatches the input, usually without keeping conversation state across turns.

explanation: The docs list five patterns: subagents, handoffs, skills, router and custom workflow. In the subagents pattern a central main agent coordinates subagents by calling them as tools; all routing passes through it, and subagents return results to it rather than to the user.

stem: LangChain's multi-agent guide advises reaching for a multi-agent design whenever a task needs more than one step.

options.text: True
options.why: Multi-step work alone is not the trigger; the docs point out that one agent with the right tools and prompt often achieves similar results.

options.text: False
options.why: The guide says not every complex task needs multi-agent: a single agent with the right (sometimes dynamic) tools and prompt can often do the job.

explanation: The docs tie multi-agent to specific needs: context management (too many tools or too much specialised knowledge for one context), distributed development by separate teams, and parallel work. A long but coherent task is usually still one agent with good tools.

stem: A deep agent created with `create_deep_agent(...)` delegates work to a subagent by calling one built-in tool, passing `description` and `subagent_type`. Type the tool's name.
explanation: The Deep Agents harness ships a built-in `task` tool. Its arguments are `description` (sent to the subagent as its first human message) and `subagent_type` (the name of the subagent). The subagent's final message comes back to the main agent as the tool result.

stem: A team is starting a new supervisor-style system in October 2026 and finds the `langgraph-supervisor` package with its `create_supervisor` helper. What do the current docs say about it?

options.text: It became part of LangGraph core in 1.x, so you now import `create_supervisor` from `langgraph.graph`.
options.why: There is no `create_supervisor` in LangGraph core; the helper only ever lived in the separate package.

options.text: It is the only supported way to build a supervisor, because a plain `create_agent` cannot call other agents.
options.why: The recommended approach is exactly a plain `create_agent` whose tools invoke the worker agents.

options.text: It is no longer actively maintained; use a `create_agent` supervisor whose tools wrap the workers.
options.why: The migration guide says this, and maps `create_supervisor` to a main `create_agent` with each worker wrapped in a `@tool` function.

options.text: It was renamed to `langgraph-swarm`, which keeps the same `create_supervisor` API and arguments.
options.why: `langgraph-swarm` is a different library for handoff-style systems, with `create_swarm`, not a renamed supervisor package.

explanation: The `langgraph-supervisor` README now recommends building the supervisor directly with tool calls because that gives more control over context engineering, and the migration guide states that the package is no longer actively maintained. The replacement is the subagents pattern: workers are `create_agent` graphs, each wrapped in a tool that invokes it and returns its final message.

stem: You call `create_deep_agent(model=m, tools=[search])` and pass no `backend`. Where do the files the agent writes with `write_file` live?

options.text: In agent state (`StateBackend`): kept across turns of one thread, not shared with other threads
options.why: `StateBackend()` is the default; files sit in the `files` state key and are checkpointed with the thread.

options.text: On the local disk under the current working directory, through `FilesystemBackend`
options.why: Disk access only happens if you pass a `FilesystemBackend` explicitly, and the docs warn against it for web servers.

options.text: In the LangGraph store, so every thread of every user can see them
options.why: Cross-thread files need a `StoreBackend` (or a route to one); that is not the default.

options.text: Nowhere: without an explicit backend the filesystem tools are simply not offered to the model at all
options.why: The filesystem tools are part of the default stack, backed by `StateBackend`.

explanation: If `backend` is omitted, Deep Agents uses `StateBackend()`. Files are stored in agent state for the current thread and survive later turns through checkpoints, but a new `thread_id` starts with no files. Use `StoreBackend` or a `CompositeBackend` route for anything that must outlive the thread.

stem: In `langgraph-swarm`, `create_handoff_tool(agent_name="Bob")` is called without a `name`. Type the name the generated tool gets.
explanation: `create_handoff_tool` names the tool `transfer_to_<agent_name>` (normalised to lower case) and gives it the description "Ask agent '<name>' for help". When called, it returns a `Command` with `graph=Command.PARENT`, `goto=<agent_name>` and an update that sets `active_agent` and appends a ToolMessage confirming the transfer.

stem: What is the main difference between a supervisor (the subagents pattern) and a router in LangChain's multi-agent docs?

options.text: A router can only ever forward a request to exactly one agent, whereas a supervisor is able to call several agents in parallel.
options.why: A router can fan out to several agents in parallel with `Send` and then combine their results.

options.text: A router has to be rule-based, whereas a supervisor always uses an LLM to decide.
options.why: The docs describe a router as often being a single LLM classification call; rules are only one option.

options.text: A supervisor is an agent that keeps context and picks subagents across turns; a router is a one-off classification step.
options.why: The docs draw exactly this distinction: a supervisor orchestrates as the conversation evolves, a router is a lightweight preprocessing step.

options.text: A supervisor needs the `langgraph-supervisor` package, whereas a router is built into `create_agent` itself.
options.why: Both are patterns you build yourself; the docs build the supervisor from plain `create_agent` plus tools.

explanation: Both patterns can send work to several agents. The supervisor is itself an agent: it keeps the conversation and can call subagents repeatedly over many turns. A router classifies the input and dispatches it, which suits clear input categories; to make it conversational, wrap it as a tool of a stateful agent.

stem: According to LangChain's context-engineering guide, what is the most common reason an agent takes the wrong action?

options.text: The temperature is set too high, so tool choice becomes random
options.why: Temperature is not the cause the guide names; it lists model capability and missing context.

options.text: The graph has too few nodes for the task
options.why: Graph size has nothing to do with the cause the guide gives.

options.text: The underlying model is not capable enough for the task
options.why: The guide lists this as one of two causes but says it is the less common one.

options.text: The right context was not passed to the model
options.why: The guide says that more often than not, failures come from the model not getting the right context.

explanation: The guide gives two reasons an LLM call inside an agent fails: the model is not capable enough, or the right context was not passed, and it says the second is more common. That is why the multi-agent docs put context engineering, deciding what each agent sees, at the centre of multi-agent design.

stem: LangChain's multi-agent docs compare patterns on a one-shot request ("buy coffee"). Handoffs, skills and router each take 3 model calls. Why does the subagents pattern take 4?

options.text: Subagents must always call a planning tool such as `write_todos` before they are allowed to call any other tool
options.why: No planning step is part of the pattern; the extra call has another cause.

options.text: The subagent's result returns to the main agent, which spends one more model call on the reply
options.why: The docs say subagents add one call because results return through the main agent, and that this overhead buys centralised control.

options.text: Each subagent first asks the user to confirm before it acts
options.why: Subagents do not talk to the user by default; they return to the main agent.

options.text: Subagents re-run a router step before every tool call they make
options.why: There is no router in the subagents pattern; the main agent itself chooses the tool.

explanation: In the subagents pattern the main agent calls the subagent tool, the subagent works (its own model calls), and its final message returns as a tool result that the main agent reads before replying. That extra hop through the supervisor is the price of centralised control and context isolation.

stem: A supervisor delegates to a `research` subagent wrapped as a tool that returns `result["messages"][-1].content`. Traces show the subagent ran five useful searches, yet the supervisor keeps replying "I could not find anything". What is the likely cause and fix?

options.text: The subagent needs its own checkpointer so it can keep its search results between calls and hand them over on the next invocation.
options.why: Persistence does not change what the tool wrapper returns; the supervisor still gets only the final message.

options.text: The tool should return the subagent's entire message list as a Python list.
options.why: Dumping the full trace bloats the supervisor's context and is the opposite of what the docs suggest.

options.text: The supervisor's recursion limit is cutting the subagent's searches short.
options.why: The searches finished, as the traces show; the problem is what comes back.

options.text: The final message lacks the findings; prompt the subagent to restate them there, since the supervisor sees only that.
options.why: The docs call this a common failure mode and recommend reminding the subagent that the supervisor only sees its final output, or formatting the output in code.

explanation: In the subagents pattern the supervisor receives whatever the wrapper returns, typically just the last message. If the subagent ends with "Done!" after its tool calls, the findings are lost. Prompt the subagent to restate the results in its final message, or build the return value in code, for example a `Command` that also passes back extra state keys.

stem: Which situations do LangChain's docs give as good reasons to split one agent into a multi-agent system? (Choose two.)

options.text: The single agent has so many tools that it often picks the wrong one
options.why: The docs call out too many tools and poor tool choice as a reason for multi-agent patterns.

options.text: Different teams need to build and maintain separate capabilities independently
options.why: Distributed development is one of the three capabilities the docs list.

options.text: The task has three sequential steps that always run in the same order
options.why: A fixed sequence is a workflow; plain graph nodes or one agent handle it without multiple agents.

options.text: More agents always lower token cost, because each prompt is shorter
options.why: The docs' cost tables show some patterns using more calls and tokens, so splitting is not automatically cheaper.

options.text: Responses would be more creative if several models answered
options.why: Creativity is not a reason the docs give; extra agents add calls and coordination cost.

explanation: The docs say multi-agent patterns help when one agent has too many tools and chooses badly, when tasks need specialised knowledge with long prompts, when sequential constraints must unlock capabilities, when separate teams own separate capabilities, and when subtasks can run in parallel. Otherwise, start with a single agent.

stem: By default, a custom Deep Agents subagent called through the `task` tool sees the main agent's full conversation history.

options.text: True
options.why: The default is `mode: "isolated"`, so the subagent sees only the task description; forking is opt-in.

options.text: False
options.why: Isolated mode is the default: the subagent starts with a single human message containing the `description`. Only `mode: "fork"` (beta) passes the parent's history.

explanation: Deep Agents subagents are isolated by default, which is how they keep the main agent's context clean: the subagent starts fresh with the delegated task and returns one final report. Setting `mode: "fork"` (beta, `deepagents>=0.7.13`) makes it continue the parent's conversation instead.

stem: With `deepagents` 0.7.30 you create `create_deep_agent(model=m)` with no middleware, subagents or backend. Which of these tools is the model NOT given?

options.text: `task`
options.why: The default `general-purpose` subagent is added automatically, so the `task` tool is present.

options.text: `grep`
options.why: `grep` is one of the default filesystem tools, together with `ls`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, `delete` and `glob`.

options.text: `write_todos`
options.why: Since v0.7 task planning is opt-in: you get `write_todos` only by passing `TodoListMiddleware()` in `middleware`.

options.text: `edit_file`
options.why: `edit_file` is part of the default filesystem tool set.

explanation: Running this agent with a fake model shows the tools `ls`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, `delete`, `glob`, `grep` and `task`. `execute` is hidden because the default `StateBackend` is not a sandbox. The docs note that task planning became opt-in in v0.7: add `TodoListMiddleware()` to get `write_todos`. Many older articles still describe planning as built in.

stem: A `langgraph-swarm` app is compiled with a checkpointer. On turn 1 the default agent Alice calls `transfer_to_bob` and Bob answers. On turn 2 the user writes again on the same `thread_id`. Which agent gets the message?

options.text: Bob: the swarm's `START` router reads the saved `active_agent` and routes there
options.why: `add_active_agent_router` adds a conditional edge from `START` that returns `state["active_agent"]`, falling back to the default agent.

options.text: Alice, because every new turn starts again at `default_active_agent`, whatever happened before
options.why: The default is used only when no agent has been active yet; after a handoff the saved `active_agent` wins.

options.text: A supervisor node, which re-classifies the new message
options.why: A swarm has no supervisor; agents hand off to each other directly.

options.text: Both agents, which run in parallel on the message
options.why: The router returns one destination, the active agent.

explanation: `create_swarm` adds a router at `START` that sends each new input to `active_agent`, which handoff tools set. With a checkpointer the value survives between turns, so the conversation resumes with Bob. The README warns that without short-term memory the swarm forgets which agent was last active.

stem: Match each requirement with the multi-agent pattern the LangChain docs recommend for it.

options.text: Subagents
options.why: A main agent calls specialised agents as tools and stays in charge.

options.text: Handoffs
options.why: A state variable such as `active_agent` or `current_step` switches which agent or configuration handles the user.

options.text: Skills
options.why: One agent loads specialised prompts and knowledge on demand.

options.text: Router
options.why: A classification step dispatches the input to one or more agents and synthesises the results.

prompts.text: A support bot must collect a warranty ID before refund tools unlock, and each stage talks to the user directly.
A coding assistant should pull in language-specific instructions only when a task needs them, without separate agents.
Calendar, email and CRM specialists must not talk to the user; one coordinator calls them, possibly in parallel, and combines the results.
A stateless knowledge-base endpoint classifies each query and queries GitHub, Notion and Slack in parallel before merging the answers.

explanation: The docs' quick guide: handoffs for sequential constraints and direct user interaction across stages; skills for one agent with many on-demand specialisations; subagents for distinct domains coordinated centrally with no direct user contact; router for clear verticals queried in parallel and synthesised, typically statelessly.

stem: A handoff tool inside the `support` agent returns `Command(goto="sales_agent", graph=Command.PARENT, update={...})`. Which `messages` update do the docs prescribe, assuming the handoff was the only tool call?

options.text: Only a `ToolMessage` saying "Transferred to sales agent", since the AIMessage is already in the parent's history
options.why: Without the AIMessage that holds the tool call, the parent's history would contain a tool response with no matching request.

options.text: The full message history of the support agent, so that sales can see every step
options.why: The docs advise against this: irrelevant internal reasoning confuses the receiving agent and costs tokens.

options.text: The `AIMessage` holding the handoff tool call plus a `ToolMessage` with the same `tool_call_id`
options.why: LLMs expect each tool call to be paired with a response, so the docs pass exactly this pair to the parent.

options.text: No messages at all, because the `goto` alone is enough to route
options.why: The receiving agent would then see an incomplete conversation, with no record of why it was called.

explanation: When handing off between agent subgraphs, the parent's history must stay valid: an AIMessage with a tool call has to be followed by a ToolMessage with the same `tool_call_id`. The docs pass just that pair and suggest summarising the sender's work in the ToolMessage content rather than forwarding its whole internal trace.

stem: Put these events of one isolated Deep Agents delegation in the order they happen.

options.text: The main agent's model emits a `task` tool call with a `description` and a `subagent_type`.
The subagent starts with a single human message containing the description.
The subagent calls its own tools until its model returns a final answer.
The subagent's final text is returned to the main agent as a `ToolMessage`.
The main agent's model runs again with that tool result in its history.

explanation: This matches a fake-model run of `deepagents` 0.7.30: the subagent's model saw only the description, its own `write_file` call never appeared in the parent's messages, and the parent received one `ToolMessage` holding the subagent's final text before its next model call.

stem: Take-home: build an inbox-triage agent that classifies each email (spam, question, meeting request), routes each class to a different action, and requires human approval before any reply or calendar invite goes out. Which graph shape fits best?

options.text: A `classify` node, a conditional edge per class, an approval interrupt before each external write, spam to `END`
options.why: Routing and the approval gate are explicit in the graph, so the model cannot skip them, and the spam path costs nothing.

options.text: One agent with all the tools and a system prompt that says "always ask before sending"
options.why: A prompt instruction is not a guarantee; the model can still call the send tool without approval.

options.text: A swarm in which every class agent can hand off to every other one, with a single human approval requested at the very end
options.why: Free handoffs make the path non-deterministic, and approving afterwards is too late for an action that has already run.

options.text: A router that classifies and then sends each email to all three action agents in parallel
options.why: Each email needs exactly one action; fanning out to all three would send wrong replies and invites.

explanation: Deterministic parts (classification result, which action, approval before writes) belong in the graph's structure; the LLM fills in classification and drafting. The docs' custom-workflow pattern mixes deterministic steps with agentic ones in exactly this way.

stem: In `langgraph-supervisor`, `create_supervisor` has an `output_mode` parameter that controls how much of a worker's history goes into the shared message list. Type its default value.
explanation: `output_mode` accepts `"full_history"` (every worker message) or `"last_message"` (only the worker's final response); the default is `"last_message"`. In the recommended subagents pattern you get the same choice by deciding what the tool wrapper returns.

stem:
What does this custom supervisor graph print? `research` was meant to report back to the supervisor.

```python
class S(TypedDict):
    results: Annotated[list, operator.add]

runs = 0
def supervisor(s) -> Command[Literal["research", "writer", "__end__"]]:
    global runs; runs += 1
    nxt = {0: "research", 1: "writer"}.get(len(s["results"]), END)
    return Command(goto=nxt)

def research(s): return {"results": ["facts"]}
def writer(s):   return {"results": ["draft"]}

b = StateGraph(S).add_node(supervisor).add_node(research).add_node(writer)
b.add_edge(START, "supervisor")
b.add_edge("research", END)
b.add_edge("writer", "supervisor")
print(b.compile().invoke({"results": []}), runs)
```

options.text: `{'results': ['facts', 'draft']} 3`
options.why: That is what happens when `research` has an edge back to `supervisor`; here it goes to `END`.

options.text: `{'results': ['facts']} 1`
options.why: The supervisor runs once and routes to `research`, which writes `facts` and then follows its edge to `END`; `writer` never runs.

options.text: `{'results': []} 1`
options.why: `research` does run and its update is applied through the reducer before the graph ends.

options.text: `GraphRecursionError`
options.why: Nothing loops here; the run ends after two steps.

explanation: Output: `{'results': ['facts']} 1`. Workers in a supervisor design must return control to the supervisor (an edge back, or a tool result in the tool-calling version) so it can decide the next step or finish. An edge to `END` cuts the loop off silently, which is a classic bug in supervisor take-homes.

stem: A supervisor's context grows by thousands of tokens per delegation and the agents start confusing each other's intermediate steps. Which changes follow the docs' context-engineering advice? (Choose two.)

options.text: Have each worker return a concise summary or structured result instead of its full trace
options.why: The docs recommend prompting subagents to return summaries, or formatting the result in code.

options.text: For handoffs between agent subgraphs, pass only the handoff AIMessage/ToolMessage pair and put any needed summary in the ToolMessage
options.why: This is the docs' handoff recipe for keeping the parent's context focused.

options.text: Append every worker's full message list to the shared history so nothing is ever lost
options.why: This is exactly what causes token blow-up and agents confusing one another's internal steps.

options.text: Leave out the ToolMessage from handoffs to save tokens
options.why: The AIMessage tool call would then have no matching response, which corrupts the history.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window and change nothing else
options.why: A bigger window postpones the problem and raises cost; the agents still see irrelevant context.

explanation: Multi-agent context engineering is about choosing what crosses agent boundaries. Return results rather than traces, keep tool-call pairs valid, and summarise where detail is not needed. Isolation is the main reason subagents help in the first place.

options.text: `GraphRecursionError` after 10 steps
options.why: That is what happens without the counter; here the cap ends the run after four steps.

options.text: `{'hops': 3, 'log': ['billing', 'tech', 'billing']}`
options.why: The node that sees `hops == 3` still runs and logs its `:stop` entry before ending.

options.text: `{'hops': 3, 'log': ['billing', 'tech', 'billing', 'tech:stop']}`
options.why: Three handoffs raise `hops` to 3; then `tech` sees the cap, logs `tech:stop` and routes to `END`.

options.text: `{'hops': 4, 'log': ['billing', 'tech', 'billing', 'tech', 'billing:stop']}`
options.why: The check happens before the increment, so `hops` never goes past 3.

explanation: Output: `{'hops': 3, 'log': ['billing', 'tech', 'billing', 'tech:stop']}`. Without the counter the same graph raises `GraphRecursionError`. A hop budget in state plus an explicit terminal route, ideally to a clarification or human step, ends handoff ping-pong deterministically; the recursion limit is only the last-resort safety net.

stem: Design a deep-research agent: a planner splits a question into N sub-queries (N known only at run time), searches run in parallel, and a synthesiser writes a cited answer from all findings. Which LangGraph design fits?

options.text: A conditional edge returning one `Send("search", ...)` per sub-query; `findings` uses `operator.add`; then synthesise
options.why: `Send` creates one search per sub-query at run time, and the reducer collects every worker's findings without write conflicts.

options.text: A fixed set of five search nodes wired in parallel with `add_edge` from the planner
options.why: Static edges cannot adapt to a run-time N; extra queries are dropped and missing ones leave idle nodes.

options.text: A loop in which the planner calls one search per super-step until the plan is used up
options.why: This is correct but sequential, so latency grows with N, which defeats the parallel requirement.

options.text: Parallel search nodes that each write their results to a plain `findings: list` state key, which the synthesiser then reads
options.why: Without a reducer, concurrent writes to the same key raise `InvalidUpdateError`.

explanation: Map-reduce with `Send` is the idiomatic fan-out for a run-time number of workers; a reducer such as `operator.add` merges their outputs, and a downstream node synthesises the answer. The router docs use the same `Send` fan-out to query several agents in parallel.

stem: Take-home: "Build a supervisor with two worker agents. The supervisor routes, workers report back to it, and it decides when to finish." The panel asks for the approach the current LangChain docs recommend. Which implementation fits?

options.text: A `create_agent` supervisor whose tools each invoke a worker agent and return its final message
options.why: This is the subagents pattern: results come back as tool results, and the supervisor's own loop decides when to stop by answering without a tool call.

options.text: `create_supervisor` from `langgraph-supervisor`, as the maintained successor of the old tutorials
options.why: The docs now say that package is no longer actively maintained and recommend the tool-calling pattern instead.

options.text: A `create_swarm` with both workers, where each worker can hand off directly to the other
options.why: A swarm has no central supervisor; agents hand off directly, so nobody owns the finish decision.

options.text: A router node that classifies the request once and sends it to one worker, which then goes to `END`
options.why: Workers never report back, so nothing can decide on further steps or combine results.

explanation: The recommended supervisor is a normal agent whose tools wrap the workers. Because tool results return to the supervisor's model, it can call another worker, call several in parallel, or finish. Use a custom `StateGraph` only when you need deterministic steps or shared state keys between levels.

stem: A Deep Agents assistant must keep user preferences under `/memories/` across conversations, while scratch notes and offloaded tool results stay inside each conversation. Which configuration meets both requirements?

options.text: `backend=StoreBackend(namespace=lambda rt: (rt.server_info.user.identity,))` and no other backend at all
options.why: Every file, including scratch notes and offloaded results, would persist across threads; the docs recommend a `StateBackend` default to keep those ephemeral.

options.text: `CompositeBackend(default=StateBackend(), routes={"/memories/": StoreBackend(...)})` plus a `store`
options.why: `/memories/` paths go to the store and persist across threads; everything else stays thread-scoped in state.

options.text: `backend=StateBackend()` together with a checkpointer on the agent
options.why: The checkpointer keeps files per thread only; a new conversation starts with no memories.

options.text: `backend=FilesystemBackend(root_dir="/data")` on the production web server
options.why: This persists everything to disk, and the docs list web servers as an inappropriate use of this backend.

explanation: `CompositeBackend` routes by path prefix, longest match first; the `store` is passed to `create_deep_agent`. In a fake-model run of 0.7.30, a file written to `/memories/prefs.md` was readable from a new thread while `/scratch.md` was not found there. The store holds it under the key `/prefs.md` because the route prefix is stripped.

stem: A tool returns a 60,000-token log. One design trims old messages to stay under the context limit; Deep Agents instead offloads results over 20,000 tokens to its virtual filesystem. What does offloading give you that trimming does not?

options.text: Lower latency, because the model can read a long log much faster from a file than from a message
options.why: Speed is not the point; the difference is whether the data can still be reached.

options.text: Data stays retrievable: a path and preview remain, and the agent can `read_file` or `grep` it
options.why: The docs describe replacing the result with a path reference and the first 10 lines, so the raw data is not lost.

options.text: The log is automatically summarised by a second, cheaper model before it is stored
options.why: Summarisation is a separate mechanism; offloading stores the raw content unchanged.

options.text: It removes the need for a checkpointer, since files live outside graph state
options.why: With the default `StateBackend` the offloaded file lives in checkpointed state, so persistence still matters.

explanation: Trimming discards information for good. Offloading keeps the context small while leaving the full data available on demand through the filesystem tools. Deep Agents also writes a text copy of the original conversation to the filesystem when it summarises, for the same reason.

stem: With the default `StateBackend`, a file that a Deep Agents subagent writes with `write_file` is still available to the main agent after the subagent finishes.

options.text: True
options.why: The docs say the backend is shared between the supervisor and its subagents, and that files a subagent writes remain in agent state.

options.text: False
options.why: Subagent messages are isolated, but the `files` state key is not: the subagent's state update is merged back into the parent.

explanation: In a fake-model run, a general-purpose subagent wrote `/notes.md`; the parent's final state listed `/notes.md` even though the subagent's `write_file` call never appeared in the parent's messages. The `task` tool returns a `Command` that applies the subagent's non-excluded state keys, such as `files`, plus one ToolMessage. Keys such as `messages` and `todos` are excluded.

stem: A phone-support flow must record warranty status, then classify the issue, then offer a fix, unlocking different tools at each stage. One model handles every stage. Which handoffs implementation do the docs recommend?

options.text: One `create_agent` with a `current_step` key, tools that advance it, and middleware that swaps prompt and tools
options.why: The docs call single agent with middleware the simpler choice for most handoff use cases.

options.text: Three separate `create_agent` subgraphs in a parent graph, connected by `Command.PARENT` handoff tools between them
options.why: The docs reserve multiple agent subgraphs for when each agent needs a bespoke implementation, which is not the case here.

options.text: A supervisor that calls three stage subagents as tools on every single turn
options.why: Stage subagents cannot talk to the user directly, and the supervisor adds a model call per turn.

options.text: A stateless router that re-classifies the stage from scratch on every message
options.why: The stage has to persist across turns; a stateless router would lose the warranty information.

explanation: The handoffs page shows both implementations and advises single agent with middleware for most cases: state carries `current_step`, tools move it forward, and `wrap_model_call` middleware reconfigures the prompt and tools before each model call. A checkpointer keeps the step across turns.

stem: Match each Deep Agents storage requirement with the backend that meets it.

options.text: `StateBackend`
options.why: Files in agent state, checkpointed per thread

options.text: `FilesystemBackend`
options.why: Real files under a root directory on local disk

options.text: `StoreBackend`
options.why: Files in a LangGraph `BaseStore`, scoped by a namespace factory

options.text: `CompositeBackend`
options.why: Routes paths to different backends by prefix

prompts.text: A local coding-assistant CLI must edit the developer's actual project files.
A scratch pad for intermediate results and offloaded tool outputs, discarded when the conversation ends.
Per-user notes that every future conversation of that user can read, on a deployment that provisions a store.
`/memories/` must persist across threads while all other paths stay thread-scoped.

explanation: `StateBackend` is the ephemeral default. `FilesystemBackend` touches real disk and suits CLIs and CI, not web servers. `StoreBackend` gives durable cross-thread storage, isolated by its namespace factory. `CompositeBackend` combines them by path prefix.

stem: A `langgraph-swarm` app with a checkpointer and `default_active_agent="Alice"` runs two user turns on one thread. Order the events.

options.text: The `START` router finds no `active_agent` yet and routes to Alice.
Alice's model calls the `transfer_to_bob` tool.
The tool's `Command(graph=Command.PARENT)` sets `active_agent` to Bob and sends control to the Bob node.
Bob answers the user and turn 1 ends.
On turn 2 the `START` router reads `active_agent` from the checkpoint and routes straight to Bob.

explanation: The swarm's router is a conditional edge from `START` that returns `state["active_agent"]` or the default. Handoff tools update `active_agent` in the parent graph and jump there, and the checkpointer carries it into the next turn.

stem: Your supervisor keeps routing billing disputes to the `tech_support` subagent. Logs show ambiguous wording but no errors. What should you try first?

options.text: Raise the supervisor's temperature so that it explores the other subagents more often when it is unsure
options.why: More randomness makes routing less predictable, not more accurate.

options.text: Add a third subagent that double-checks every routing decision
options.why: This adds cost and latency without fixing why the descriptions are confusing.

options.text: Merge all subagents into one agent that has every tool
options.why: This brings back the tool-confusion problem that multi-agent was meant to solve.

options.text: Make subagent descriptions specific and distinct, then build a routing eval set from misrouted traces
options.why: The docs call names and descriptions the main lever the main agent uses to choose subagents.

explanation: The Deep Agents troubleshooting guide fixes "wrong subagent being selected" by making descriptions clearly distinct, for example when to use one subagent versus another. Capture the misrouted cases from traces as a dataset so you can check that the fix holds and does not break other routes.

stem: Which statements about `create_deep_agent` in `deepagents` 0.7.30 are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Tools passed through `tools=` are added to the built-in tools, not used instead of them
options.why: The docstring says passing tools is additive and never removes a built-in.

options.text: A `general-purpose` subagent is added automatically unless you supply one with that name or disable it through the harness profile
options.why: This is why the `task` tool exists even when you pass no `subagents`.

options.text: It returns an object that is not a LangGraph graph, so checkpointers cannot be attached
options.why: It returns a compiled LangGraph `StateGraph` and accepts `checkpointer=` and `store=`.

options.text: `write_todos` planning is always included
options.why: Planning has been opt-in since v0.7, through `TodoListMiddleware`.

options.text: The `execute` tool runs shell commands with the default `StateBackend`
options.why: `execute` needs a sandbox backend; with `StateBackend` it is not offered.

explanation: Deep Agents is a harness built on `create_agent` middleware: filesystem middleware, subagent middleware with an auto-added `general-purpose` subagent, summarisation and tool-call patching, plus your middleware. The result is a compiled LangGraph graph, so persistence, streaming and interrupts work as usual.

stem: In the subagents pattern, a subagent is wrapped as a `@tool`. Which techniques do the docs show for controlling the context that crosses the boundary? (Choose two.)

options.text: Read `runtime.state["messages"]` through `ToolRuntime` and pass a transformed history to the subagent when it needs prior context
options.why: The docs' subagent-inputs example does this; passing only the query keeps the subagent isolated.

options.text: Return a `Command` whose update carries extra state keys plus a `ToolMessage` with the matching `tool_call_id`
options.why: This is the docs' subagent-outputs example for passing back more than the final text.

options.text: Have the subagent write straight into the supervisor's checkpoint with `update_state`
options.why: The docs do not show this, and it bypasses the tool-call/response pairing.

options.text: Set `graph=Command.PARENT` in the subagent's tool so it takes over the supervisor's conversation
options.why: That is the handoff mechanism, which transfers control instead of returning a result to the caller.

options.text: Use `output_mode="full_history"` on `create_agent`
options.why: `output_mode` belongs to `create_supervisor`; `create_agent` has no such parameter.

explanation: Inputs: decide how much of the parent's state the subagent receives (query only for isolation, history to continue work). Outputs: return text, or a `Command` that also updates parent state keys while still answering the tool call with a ToolMessage.

stem: A deep agent (fake model, `TodoListMiddleware` added) receives one user message. Its model writes a todo, then delegates. The general-purpose subagent writes `/notes.md` and replies "Capital is Paris; notes in /notes.md". The parent then answers "Final: Paris". Which statement about the result is true?

options.text: The parent's messages include the subagent's `write_file` call and its ToolMessage, then "Final: Paris"
options.why: The subagent's internal messages never reach the parent; `messages` is excluded from the state merged back.

options.text: The subagent's model saw the user's original message and the todo-list ToolMessage before the task description
options.why: In isolated mode the subagent's only input message is the `description`.

options.text: The parent ends with a ToolMessage of the subagent's final text, then "Final: Paris"; `files` has `/notes.md`
options.why: The run shows exactly this: one ToolMessage for the `task` call, the final answer, and the subagent's file merged into parent state.

options.text: `files` is empty, because subagent state is thrown away when the subagent finishes
options.why: Non-excluded keys such as `files` are applied back to the parent through the `Command` that `task` returns.

explanation: The `task` tool invokes the subagent with the parent's state minus excluded keys (`messages`, `todos`, `structured_response` and others) and `messages=[HumanMessage(description)]`. It then returns `Command(update={...non-excluded changed keys..., "messages": [ToolMessage(final_text)]})`. Running this setup confirmed that the subagent's model saw only "Find the capital of France and save notes".

stem: During a migration off `langgraph-supervisor`, a worker's tool calls `interrupt()` to wait for an external job. The new design has a top-level `create_agent` supervisor whose tool invokes a worker `create_agent`. The callback must resume the run with `Command(resume=result)`. Which setup follows the documented propagation rules?

options.text: Compile every layer with its own `InMemorySaver`, so that each layer can pause and resume independently
options.why: The docs say to leave subagents without a checkpointer so they inherit the parent's at run time.

options.text: A checkpointer on the outermost graph only, none on subagents, and a `thread_id` on the outer call
options.why: These are the two documented rules, and they apply to any nesting depth.

options.text: Compile no layer with a checkpointer and pass the interrupt id to `invoke` instead
options.why: Without a checkpointer nothing can be paused and resumed.

options.text: Resume by calling the worker agent directly with `Command(resume=...)`
options.why: The interrupt surfaces as `__interrupt__` on the outer graph, so you resume through that graph's thread.

explanation: The `interrupt` bubbles up through the tool-wrapped `create_agent` layers to the outermost graph. Running this with fake models gave `__interrupt__` on the outer result, and after resuming the outer graph the worker finished and the supervisor answered. Inner checkpointers are not needed and change persistence semantics.

stem: System design: a production customer-support system with order lookups, refunds and escalation to humans. Which design choices hold up? (Choose three.)

options.text: Put escalation and refund approval in explicit graph structure, such as a routing node and an interrupt before the refund tool, not only in prompt text
options.why: Control flow in the graph is guaranteed; a prompt instruction can be ignored by the model.

options.text: Give each agent or stage only the tools it needs, with the least-privileged credentials
options.why: The Deep Agents docs advise minimal tool sets for focus and security, and least privilege limits damage from a bad call.

options.text: Use one `thread_id` per customer conversation, persisted with a checkpointer, and trace every model and tool call
options.why: This gives resumable, isolated conversations and the observability needed to debug misroutes.

options.text: Give one agent every tool, including the admin refund API, and tell it to be careful
options.why: This combines tool confusion with excessive privilege.

options.text: Share a single `thread_id` across customers so the bot learns faster
options.why: This leaks one customer's history into another's conversation.

options.text: Let the model decide on its own whether to escalate, with no deterministic fallback
options.why: Escalation is a policy decision that needs a guaranteed path, especially for low-confidence cases.

explanation: Interviewers look for deterministic policy in the graph (routing, approvals, escalation), least privilege per agent, per-conversation persistence and full tracing. Use the LLM for language and judgement inside guard rails, not as the guard rail.

stem: Multi-tenant agent platform: a Deep Agents app on LangSmith Deployment stores long-term files with `StoreBackend`. Users of the same assistant must never see each other's files. Which configuration enforces this?

options.text: `StoreBackend(namespace=lambda rt: (rt.server_info.assistant_id,))`
options.why: The docs describe the per-assistant namespace as storage shared by all users of that assistant.

options.text: `StoreBackend(namespace=lambda rt: (rt.execution_info.thread_id,))`
options.why: This isolates users but also cuts each user off from their own earlier conversations, which defeats long-term storage.

options.text: A shared namespace plus a system-prompt rule to read only the current user's files
options.why: A prompt is not access control; one injected instruction could read another tenant's files.

options.text: `StoreBackend(namespace=lambda rt: (rt.server_info.user.identity,))`
options.why: A namespace derived from the authenticated identity isolates data per user at the storage layer.

explanation: The namespace factory receives the `Runtime` and decides where reads and writes go. The docs give per-user, per-assistant and per-thread examples, and warn that multi-user deployments must always set a namespace factory; you can combine the identity with a tenant id for finer scopes. In 0.7.30 `namespace` is a required keyword argument: `StoreBackend()` raises `TypeError`.

stem: A deep agent is created with `interrupt_on={"delete_records": True}`. The `delete_records` tool is also used by a `CompiledSubAgent` whose runnable is a `create_agent` built separately with no HITL configuration. When that subagent calls `delete_records`, what happens?

options.text: It runs without pausing; compiled subagents don't inherit top-level `interrupt_on`
options.why: The `create_deep_agent` docstring says exactly this; only declarative `SubAgent` specs inherit `interrupt_on`.

options.text: It pauses, because `interrupt_on` applies to every tool call made anywhere in the agent tree, subagents included
options.why: Inheritance covers declarative subagents only; compiled runnables are used as provided.

options.text: Agent creation fails, because one tool cannot appear in both the parent and a subagent
options.why: Sharing a tool is allowed; nothing is validated across the two.

options.text: It pauses only if the subagent spec also sets `mode: "fork"` to share context
options.why: Fork mode controls context inheritance, not human-in-the-loop configuration.

explanation: Declarative `SubAgent` dictionaries inherit top-level `interrupt_on` unless they set their own. `CompiledSubAgent` and remote `AsyncSubAgent` specs do not, because they are pre-built. This is an easy way to leave a destructive tool ungated in a multi-agent tree.

stem: A chat product handles about 1 million single-domain requests a day. Users often repeat or refine the same request in the same conversation, and the flow must enforce "verify the account before changing the plan". Based on the docs' cost comparison, which pattern fits best?

options.text: Subagents, because context isolation always gives the lowest cost per request, including repeated ones
options.why: Subagents are stateless, so a repeat request runs the full flow again (4 + 4 calls in the docs' example).

options.text: Router, because a routing step is the cheapest thing you can run
options.why: A stateless router pays the routing call on every turn and does not enforce stage order across turns.

options.text: Handoffs: the active step persists across turns and its transitions enforce the order
options.why: The docs show handoffs saving a call on repeats (5 calls versus 8 for subagents) and recommend them for sequential constraints.

options.text: Skills, because loading skill text into context is always the cheapest option
options.why: Skills also save on repeats, but give no way to enforce the verification-before-change order.

explanation: In the docs' tables, stateful patterns (handoffs, skills) save 40–50% of calls on repeat requests, while subagents keep a constant per-request cost. Only handoffs also enforce sequential constraints, through tools that move a `current_step` or `active_agent` state value.

stem: Senior take-home: a turn-based multi-agent simulation (a debate between three persona agents) needs controlled turn-taking, a shared transcript, resumable sessions and replayable logs. Which design fits best?

options.text: Give each persona its own `thread_id` and checkpointer, then merge the three transcripts by timestamp when the debate ends
options.why: Separate threads break the shared transcript and make the turn order impossible to replay as one session.

options.text: Personas hand off to each other with swarm-style handoff tools, and the LLM picks the next speaker
options.why: Model-chosen handoffs make turn order non-deterministic and prone to ping-pong.

options.text: Keep the transcript in a module-level Python list that every node appends to
options.why: Global state is not checkpointed, so it can be neither resumed nor replayed, and it leaks between sessions.

options.text: A moderator node picks the speaker; reducer-backed transcript; one checkpointed thread per session; `get_state_history`
options.why: Turn order is deterministic, the transcript accumulates safely, and every step is checkpointed for resume and replay.

explanation: Simulations are a custom workflow: deterministic control (whose turn, for example round-robin from a turn counter) belongs in the graph, the agents produce the content. Checkpoints after each step give session persistence, and the state history provides a replayable log.

stem: Which statements about context compression in Deep Agents are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: A tool result over the token threshold (20,000 by default) is written to the backend and replaced by a file path plus a preview of its first lines
options.why: The docs describe this offloading, with a 10-line preview, and the agent can read or grep the file later.

options.text: When it summarises, the agent also writes a text copy of the original messages to the filesystem as a canonical record
options.why: The docs call this filesystem preservation, so details stay recoverable after the in-context summary.

options.text: Summarisation is off by default and needs `SummarizationMiddleware` to be added
options.why: Every `create_deep_agent` call includes `SummarizationMiddleware` in its base stack.

options.text: Offloading only works with `FilesystemBackend`
options.why: Offloading goes to whichever backend is configured; the docs recommend `StateBackend` as the default so these artifacts stay ephemeral.

options.text: The main agent receives each subagent's full tool trace so nothing is lost
options.why: Subagents return one final report; isolating the trace is the point.

explanation: Deep Agents layers compression: offload large tool inputs and results to files, then summarise once the context crosses about 85% of the model's `max_input_tokens` and nothing more can be offloaded, keeping a canonical text copy on the filesystem. Subagents isolate heavy work on top of that.

options.text: `{'log': ['alice', "bob saw keys ['log', 'task_description']"]}`
options.why: The parent has no `task_description` channel, so that part of the update cannot be stored or passed to Bob.

options.text: `InvalidUpdateError` because the parent has no `task_description` key
options.why: Running it raises nothing; the unknown key is dropped silently.

options.text: `{'log': ['alice', "bob saw keys ['log']"]}`
options.why: The `log` update is applied in the parent and Bob runs, but `task_description` disappears because the parent schema lacks it.

options.text: `{'log': ["bob saw keys ['log']"]}`
options.why: Alice's `log` update is applied through the parent's reducer before Bob runs.

explanation: A `Command.PARENT` update is applied to the parent graph's channels. A key the parent does not declare is silently lost, so the handoff payload never reaches the next agent. The swarm README warns that both the multi-agent graph and the next agent must have every key you put in `Command.update`.

stem: A coordinator dispatches to many subagents built by different teams. Which statements about the docs' single dispatch tool design (one `task(agent_name, description)` tool) are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: New agents can be added through a registry without changing the coordinator's tool list, which suits distributed teams
options.why: The docs list scalable addition of agents and team distribution as reasons to choose a single dispatch tool.

options.text: For a large or frequently changing registry, a discovery tool such as `list_agents` lets the coordinator find agents on demand instead of listing them all in the prompt
options.why: The docs recommend tool-based discovery for more than about 10 agents or dynamic registries.

options.text: It gives more per-agent control over inputs and outputs than one tool per agent
options.why: The docs say the opposite: it trades per-agent context engineering for simpler composition.

options.text: It requires all subagents to share the coordinator's message history
options.why: By convention, the task description is passed as a single human message and the final message comes back.

options.text: An enum on `agent_name` is the best choice for a registry that changes weekly
options.why: The docs say an enum needs a code change whenever agents change, so it suits small, static lists.

explanation: Tool per agent gives fine-grained control. The single dispatch tool gives convention-based composition, strong context isolation and easy extension. For discovery, use system-prompt enumeration or an enum for small static sets and a discovery tool for large or dynamic registries.

stem: Match each declarative Deep Agents `SubAgent` field setting with how it behaves.

options.text: Inherits the main agent's value
options.why: Used when the field is left out

options.text: Replaces the parent's value entirely
options.why: No merging with the parent's list

options.text: Receives the parent's conversation history
options.why: Context inheritance instead of isolation

options.text: Is not inherited, so isolated subagents should define their own
options.why: The docs list it as required for custom isolated subagents

prompts.text: `permissions` set to a list of rules

explanation: From the Deep Agents subagent docs and source: omitted `tools`, `model` and `interrupt_on` are inherited; a `permissions` list replaces the parent's rules entirely; `mode: "fork"` (beta) continues the parent's conversation; an isolated subagent does not inherit the main agent's `system_prompt`, so it should define its own.

stem: Order the stages Deep Agents goes through as a long session's context grows, from first to last.

options.text: A single tool result over the token threshold is written to the backend and replaced by a path plus a short preview.
As the context crosses about 85% of the model's input window, older large tool-call inputs (such as full file writes) are truncated to pointers.
When nothing more can be offloaded, older history is summarised and a text copy of the original messages is saved to the filesystem.
The agent uses `read_file` or `grep` on the saved files to recover details it needs later.

explanation: Offloading happens first (large results at write time, large inputs once the 85% mark is crossed). Summarisation runs only when context is still over the limit and nothing more can be offloaded. Because both steps leave files behind, the agent can fetch exact details back on demand.
